This is a course with a workshop at its centre. The workshop runs as a single day of four 90-minute parts. The same case and the same exercise are also used in longer deliveries, over three days or across a semester, and a reader studying alone can work through them at their own pace. The tracks below set out the four scales and say what to do at each.

The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: retrieving data from an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text.

These skills are taught through an applied 'replication' exercise. Participants reproduce one of the reanalyses that made up the Multi100 project, whose results appeared in *Nature* [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The reanalysis focuses on selected results from a *European Sociological Review* article by @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, testing the statistical robustness of a claim made by the original author (OA).

@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic explored how the European Union (EU) was framed across 27 member states, and the selected claim from the paper is that "…poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619]. This claim has been tested by five analysts for the Multi100 project, and in this course you will be testing their results. You will:

1. **Reproduce a published analyst's result.** Run the submitted Multi100 analysis code on the original re-analysis data and find the exact coefficient it produced.
2. **See why five analysts got five different answers.** When you run the same code, you should get the same results; but there are different analysis options to choose from, and the five analysts each made different choices. Working through different analysis options involves engaging with and choosing between various statistical methods.
3. **State an _estimand_ and draw a causal graph.** Often, variation in methods and therefore results is driven by having an imprecise understanding of the *quantity* that the study is trying to estimate. That quantity is the *estimand*. Thinking about estimands is, first of all, a conceptual matter, as is thinking about the real-life relationships between the variables in your dataset. Causal graphs, or directed acyclic graphs or DAGs, are a useful way to visualise these relationships and decide what variables to adjust for.
4. **Preregister one specification.** Pick one defensible analysis from a menu of choices. Before you run it, fill in the preregistration block of your report, which is a shortened version of a real preregistration template: the claim you are testing, one option for each decision on the menu, and a sentence grounded in your causal graph on why you adjust for what you do.
5. **Run it and submit the result.** Your result appears as a point on a live chart, against the curve of the claim and, in a taught session, beside everyone else in the class.
6. **Read a specification curve.** Work out what the 864 specifications of the curve of the claim, taken together, can and cannot establish.

The exercise follows the design of Multi100 on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared. The [case study](case/index.qmd) presents the original paper, the SCORE programme and the Multi100 project, and the five reanalyses, and every track starts there.

## The tracks

| Track | Who it is for |
|---|---|
| [One day – open science and replication](tracks/one-day-replication/index.qmd) | A group with a day and a facilitator, and the reproducibility of published research as the reason for meeting. Four 90-minute parts with breaks between them – the format for which the course was built. |
| [One day – social data science tools](tracks/one-day-tools/index.qmd) | The same day with the toolchain in the foreground: the IDE, the document format, packages, version control and where finished work is archived, with a first session in R inside the day. |
| [One day – the statistical methods](tracks/one-day-methods/index.qmd) | The same day with the statistics in the foreground: the causal graph in full, the decisions of the specification menu that set the question and the model, each shown doing something to an estimate, and the multiverse read in detail. |
| [Three days](tracks/three-days/index.qmd) | A group that wants the tools underneath the exercise and the methods behind it. A tools day, then the workshop, then a methods day. |
| [Semester](tracks/semester/index.qmd) | A taught module or a research-training programme that runs across a term. Ten sessions, with the workshop day placed partway through the term as its practical core. |
| [Self-study](tracks/self-study/index.qmd) | A reader working alone, at their own pace. The companion modules and the exercise ordered into a route that needs neither a facilitator nor a cohort. |

Each track is an ordered route through pages already on this site, with a sidebar of its own and, at the end, the slide deck that the track uses. What changes between them is the pace, the balance, and how much of the surrounding material comes with the workshop. A scheduled delivery can name one of these six tracks, and when it does, the callout at the top of this page links to that track.

## Running the analyses {#two-routes-one-destination}

The exercise is the same in every track, and it is done in R. Install R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) once, before the day, then download a ready-made workspace – a single zip file holding the analysis code, the data and a report to fill in. There is nothing to configure and no account to create, so you open the folder and start working, and the workspace is yours to keep afterwards. The [Setup](setup.qmd) page walks you through the installation in plain steps.

The [Browser lab](exercise/browser-lab.qmd) page holds the same exercise and the same data on a version of R that runs inside a browser tab, with nothing installed. It is the page on which the facilitator demonstrates on a shared screen, the place to try R and the data before you have installed anything, and the fallback if a machine fails on the day. Anyone can use it, whether or not they are taking the course.

## The workshop day {#four-blocks-ninety-minutes-each}

The workshop has this structure on the one-day course in open science and replication and in session 9 of the semester track. The tools-focused and methods-focused one-day formats keep four 90-minute parts but divide the material differently, and the three-day track teaches the first part on day 1 and runs the other three across the four sessions of day 2. Two breaks and a lunch separate the parts. When a delivery is scheduled, the callout at the top of this page gives its clock times.

| Part | Length | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Part 1 – Credibility and tools | 90 minutes | What social science is for and why people say it is in crisis; what open research proposes; the three Rs (reproducibility, robustness, replicability) and the evidence on each; and the computational toolchain that makes any of it checkable. |
| Break | | |
| Part 2 – The claim and its estimand | 90 minutes | The EU-frames paper in full, and why analysts who look like they disagree are often answering different questions. Estimands, causal graphs, and a DAG for the EU-frames case, which you finish yourself. |
| Lunch | | |
| Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration | 90 minutes | Reproducing the published result exactly, then working through the specification menu: what each analytical choice does, and what happens to the estimate when you change one. |
| Break | | |
| Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration | 90 minutes | Reading the results from the class against the curve of the claim, on which the five reanalyses and the original study are marked; what a curve can and cannot establish; and settling on the one analysis you would defend, preregistered before you run it. |

---

## The companion curriculum

The [companion curriculum](companion/index.qmd) holds the teaching material of the course, arranged in three strands: computational tools, data management and sharing, and statistical methods. Every module keeps its own page and stands on its own, so you can read one for the skill it covers or take it in the place that a track gives it.

A single day has room for the exercise and very little else, which is why a one-day track points to the modules rather than working through them. The longer tracks are built out of them. The three-day track spends a day on the tools underneath the exercise and a day on the methods behind it, the semester track spreads the same modules across a term, and the self-study track puts them in an order that needs no facilitator at all.
